Appendix A Appendix

A.0 Notation & Shapes

Refer to Table 6

A.1 Stacked SVD: Shared Right Subspace and Global Optimum (Proof)

When multiple modules share the same input dimension, we vertically concatenate the module-wise error matrices 𝐄𝒊∈ℝ𝑶𝒊×𝒅\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{O}_{\bm{i}}\times\bm{d}} into 𝐄cat\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}. We then choose a shared right subspace (the row space of 𝐁\mathbf{B}) while allowing module-specific left factors 𝐀𝒊\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}, by solving

min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁‖F2.\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\ \bigl\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}.

This appendix shows that (i) the solution is well-defined, and (ii) the shared 𝐁\mathbf{B} is also optimal in an energy/projection sense (Ky Fan; cf. Fan (1950); Golub and Van Loan (2013)). Consequently, a single shared 𝐁\mathbf{B} serves as a strong representative of what one might otherwise try to learn as separate 𝐁𝒊\mathbf{B}_{\bm{i}}’s per module.

Problem (Unweighted Frobenius Approximation).
min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁‖F2.\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\ \bigl\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}. (A.1.1)

Lemma A.1.1 - Equivalence of Search Sets: ℳ𝒓=ℛ𝒓\mathcal{M}_{\bm{r}}=\mathcal{R}_{\bm{r}}.

Let

ℳ𝒓:={𝐀𝐁:𝐀∈ℝ𝒎×𝒓,𝐁∈ℝ𝒓×𝒅},ℛ𝒓:={𝐗∈ℝ𝒎×𝒅:rank(𝐗)≤𝒓}.\mathcal{M}_{\bm{r}}:=\{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}:\ \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{m}\times\bm{r}},\ \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{d}}\},\qquad\mathcal{R}_{\bm{r}}:=\{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{m}\times\bm{d}}:\ \mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})\leq\bm{r}\}.

Then ℳ𝒓=ℛ𝒓\mathcal{M}_{\bm{r}}=\mathcal{R}_{\bm{r}}.

This is a standard consequence of rank-factorization and the SVD characterization of best rank-𝒓\bm{r} approximants; see, e.g., Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960); Golub and Van Loan (2013); Horn and Johnson (1985). We omit the proof.

Proof.

By Lemma A.1.1, the problem reduces to a rank-𝒓\bm{r} approximation of 𝐄cat\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}. By the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960), the optimizer is the truncated SVD

𝐗⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤,\mathbf{X}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top},

so any global minimizer (𝐀,𝐁)(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}) must satisfy

𝐀𝐁=𝐗⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤.\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{X}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}. (A.1.2)

If 𝝈𝒓=𝝈𝒓+1\bm{\sigma}_{\bm{r}}=\bm{\sigma}_{\bm{r}+1}, the optimizer may be non-unique Golub and Van Loan (2013). ∎

Theorem A.1.2 - Identifying the Shared Right Subspace: row⁡(𝐁)=span⁡(𝐕𝒓⊤)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B})=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}).

We determine the optimal shared right subspace for the factorization min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁‖F2\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\ \|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2}. Let 𝐄cat=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} be a thin SVD, and let r=rank⁡(𝐁)r=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B}). Denote 𝐒:=row⁡(𝐁)\mathbf{S}:=\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}) and the orthogonal projector 𝐏𝐒:=𝐁⊤​(𝐁𝐁⊤)−1​𝐁\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}:=\mathbf{B}^{\top}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{B} (assume 𝐁\mathbf{B} has full row rank; otherwise use the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse).

Fixing 𝐁\mathbf{B}, least-squares normal equations yield (see, e.g., (Golub and Van Loan, 2013, §5))

𝐀∗\displaystyle\mathbf{A}^{\ast} =𝐄cat​𝐁⊤​(𝐁𝐁⊤)−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\mathbf{B}^{\top}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top})^{-1}, (A.1.3a)
𝐀∗​𝐁\displaystyle\mathbf{A}^{\ast}\mathbf{B} =𝐄cat​𝐏𝐒.\displaystyle=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}. (A.1.3b)

Hence, with 𝐆:=𝐄cat⊤​𝐄cat\mathbf{G}:=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}},

‖𝐄cat−𝐀∗​𝐁‖F2=‖𝐄cat​(𝐈−𝐏𝐒)‖F2=‖𝐄cat‖F2−tr⁡(𝐏𝐒​𝐆),\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}^{\ast}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2}=\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}})\|_{F}^{2}=\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\|_{F}^{2}-\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\mathbf{G}), (A.1.4)

where the last identity is the usual projection-trace formula (cf. Horn and Johnson (1985)).

Therefore, selecting 𝐒\mathbf{S} of dimension rr is equivalent to

maxdim𝐒=r⁡tr⁡(𝐏𝐒​𝐆).\max_{\dim\mathbf{S}=r}\ \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\mathbf{G}). (A.1.5)

By Ky Fan’s maximum principle Fan (1950), the maximizer 𝐒\mathbf{S} is the span of the top-rr eigenvectors of 𝐆\mathbf{G}. Since 𝐄cat=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} implies 𝐆=𝐕​𝚺2​𝐕⊤\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{V}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}\mathbf{V}^{\top}, its top-rr eigenspace equals span⁡(𝐕r)\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{r}). Thus

row⁡(𝐁)=span⁡(𝐕𝒓⊤).\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B})=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}). (A.1.6)

∎

Theorem A.1.3 - Representativeness / Energy Optimality: Sum of Projection Energies.

The shared right subspace 𝐒=row⁡(𝐁)\mathbf{S}=\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}) of dimension rr maximizes the total projection energy ∑i‖𝐄i​𝐏𝐒‖F2\sum_{i}\|\mathbf{E}_{i}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\|_{F}^{2}, where 𝐏𝐒\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}} is the orthogonal projector onto 𝐒\mathbf{S} (e.g., 𝐏𝐒=𝐐𝐐⊤\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} for any orthonormal basis 𝐐\mathbf{Q} of 𝐒\mathbf{S}).

Proof.

For each module 𝐄i\mathbf{E}_{i},

‖𝐄i​𝐏𝐒‖F2=tr⁡(𝐏𝐒​𝐄i⊤​𝐄i),\|\mathbf{E}_{i}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}\!\bigl(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\,\mathbf{E}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{i}\bigr), (A.1.7)

a standard identity using symmetry/idempotence of 𝐏𝐒\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}} and trace cyclicity (see, e.g., Horn and Johnson (1985); Golub and Van Loan (2013)). Summing over ii yields

max⁡∑idim𝐒=r⁡‖𝐄i​𝐏𝐒‖F2=maxdim𝐒=r⁡tr⁡(𝐏𝐒​∑i𝐄i⊤​𝐄i)=maxdim𝐒=r⁡tr⁡(𝐏𝐒​𝐆),𝐆:=∑i𝐄i⊤​𝐄i=𝐄cat⊤​𝐄cat.\max_{\dim\mathbf{S}=r}\ \sum_{i}\|\mathbf{E}_{i}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\|_{F}^{2}\;=\;\max_{\dim\mathbf{S}=r}\ \mathrm{tr}\!\Bigl(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\sum_{i}\mathbf{E}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{i}\Bigr)\;=\;\max_{\dim\mathbf{S}=r}\ \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\mathbf{G}),\quad\mathbf{G}:=\sum_{i}\mathbf{E}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{i}=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}. (A.1.8)

By Ky Fan’s maximum principle Fan (1950) (cf. Eq. A.1.5), the maximizer is the span of the top-rr eigenvectors of 𝐆\mathbf{G}. Since 𝐄cat=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} implies 𝐆=𝐕​𝚺2​𝐕⊤\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{V}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}\mathbf{V}^{\top}, it follows that

𝐒∗=span(𝐕r)⟺row(𝐁)=span(𝐕r⊤).\mathbf{S}^{\ast}=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{r})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B})=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{r}^{\top}).

∎

Lemma A.1.4 - Identifiability and “Balanced” Factorization.

Although the pair (𝐀,𝐁)(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}) is non-unique up to invertible reparameterizations, the right subspace row⁡(𝐁)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}) is identifiable; choosing the SVD half-split 𝚺𝒓1/2\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2} yields a numerically stable balanced factorization Golub and Van Loan (2013).

Non-uniqueness.

For any invertible 𝐑∈ℝ𝒓×𝒓\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{r}},

(𝐀,𝐁)↦(𝐀𝐑,𝐑−1​𝐁)⇒𝐀𝐁​invariant.(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})\mapsto(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{R},\ \mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{B})\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\ \text{invariant}.

Hence factors are not unique, while the projector onto row⁡(𝐁)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}) is unique (right singular subspace; cf. Theorem. A.1.2 and Golub and Van Loan (2013)).

Balanced factorization.

Let 𝐄cat=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} and denote by 𝐔𝒓,𝚺𝒓,𝐕𝒓\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}} the top-𝒓\bm{r} blocks. The half-split

𝐀∗\displaystyle\mathbf{A}^{\ast} =𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓1/2,\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}, (A.1.9a)
𝐁∗\displaystyle\mathbf{B}^{\ast} =𝚺𝒓1/2​𝐕𝒓⊤,\displaystyle=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}, (A.1.9b)
𝐀∗​𝐁∗\displaystyle\mathbf{A}^{\ast}\mathbf{B}^{\ast} =𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top} (A.1.9c)

satisfies

𝐀∗⁣⊤​𝐀∗=𝚺𝒓,𝐁∗​𝐁∗⁣⊤=𝚺𝒓,\mathbf{A}^{\ast\top}\mathbf{A}^{\ast}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},\qquad\mathbf{B}^{\ast}\mathbf{B}^{\ast\top}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},

which avoids squaring condition numbers in normal equations and minimizes combined factor norms among reparameterizations:

12​(‖𝐀‖F2+‖𝐁‖F2)≥‖𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤‖∗,\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}^{2}+\|\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\ \geq\ \|\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\|_{\ast},

with equality at (𝐀∗,𝐁∗)(\mathbf{A}^{\ast},\mathbf{B}^{\ast}) Recht et al. (2010). (Standard facts; see Golub and Van Loan (2013); Recht et al. (2010).)

Block Recovery and the Pseudoinverse

Given the shared right factor 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{\ast}, each module-specific left factor 𝐀𝒊\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}} is obtained by a single least-squares solve. Using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse provides the minimum-norm solution and remains valid under rank deficiency Penrose (1955); Ben-Israel and Greville (2010); Golub and Van Loan (2013):

𝐀𝒊∗=𝐄𝒊​𝐁∗⁣⊤​(𝐁∗​𝐁∗⁣⊤)†.\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\ast}=\ \mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}\,\mathbf{B}^{{\ast}\top}\,\bigl(\mathbf{B}^{\ast}\mathbf{B}^{{\ast}\top}\bigr)^{\bm{\dagger}}. (A.1.10)

It suggests that (i) when 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{\ast} has full row rank, (⋅)†(\cdot)^{\bm{\dagger}} reduces to the inverse and Eq. A.1.10 coincides with the normal-equations solution; (ii) in general, (⋅)†(\cdot)^{\bm{\dagger}} yields the unique minimum-norm LS solution and is numerically stable under near-singularity Ben-Israel and Greville (2010); Golub and Van Loan (2013).

A.2 Covariance-Aligned Objective: Bridge Equivalence and Global Minimizer (Proof)

Sec. 3.1.2 formulates the covariance-aligned objective

min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2,\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\,\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2},

which weights errors by the input usage encoded in the covariance 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} Anderson (1984); Bishop (2006). This appendix provides a complete mathematical justification: (i) a bridge equivalence that converts 𝔼⁡[‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝐱‖22]\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\|\!(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\mathbf{x}\!\|_{2}^{2}\bigr] into a Frobenius form via the trace identity 𝔼⁡[𝐱⊤​𝐌𝐱]=tr⁡(𝐌​𝚺𝐱)\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}]=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}) Petersen and Pedersen (2006); (ii) a whitening reduction to a standard low-rank approximation by the change of variables 𝐁~:=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}:=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} (and 𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} on the right) Golub and Van Loan (2013); (iii) a closed-form global minimizer given by the truncated SVD of 𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} with balanced factors and the identity of the shared right subspace; and (iv) extensions to nonzero-mean inputs (centering) and singular 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} via pseudoinverse whitening Ben-Israel and Greville (2010); Penrose (1955).

In our case, the (distribution-weighted) risk is the expected squared output error under the input law:

ℛ⁡(𝐀,𝐁):=𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22.\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}):=\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}.

Directions used more frequently or with larger magnitude (large variance) are weighted more heavily by 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}, which motivates a right-weighted objective via 𝚺𝐱1/2\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} Bishop (2006); Anderson (1984). An empirical counterpart uses samples {𝐱𝒏}𝒏=1𝑵\{\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}\}_{\bm{n}=1}^{\bm{N}}:

ℛ^​(𝐀,𝐁):=1𝑵​∑𝒏=1𝑵‖𝐌​𝐱𝒏‖22,𝚺^𝐱:=1𝑵​∑𝒏=1𝑵𝐱𝒏​𝐱𝒏⊤.\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}):=\frac{1}{\bm{N}}\sum_{\bm{n}=1}^{\bm{N}}\|\mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}:=\frac{1}{\bm{N}}\sum_{\bm{n}=1}^{\bm{N}}\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}^{\top}.

Theorem A.2.1 (Bridge equivalence).

In this subsection, we prove the bridge identity 𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22=tr⁡(𝐌​𝚺𝐱​𝐌⊤)=‖𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{M}^{\top})=\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}, which converts the distribution-weighted risk into a Frobenius norm amenable to SVD analysis (see the trace/expectation identities in Petersen and Pedersen (2006)).

For zero-mean inputs with covariance 𝚺𝐱⪰𝟎\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\succeq\mathbf{0},

𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22=tr⁡(𝐌​𝚺𝐱​𝐌⊤)=‖𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2.\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{M}^{\top})=\bigl\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

(Vector norm →\to trace). Since ‖𝐲‖22=tr⁡(𝐲𝐲⊤)\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^{\top}) and trace is linear,

𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22=𝔼​tr⁡(𝐌𝐱𝐱⊤​𝐌⊤)=tr⁡(𝐌​𝔼​[𝐱𝐱⊤]​𝐌⊤)=tr⁡(𝐌​𝚺𝐱​𝐌⊤).\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\,\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{M}^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\mathbf{M}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}]\,\mathbf{M}^{\top}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{M}^{\top}).

(Trace →\to Frobenius). Because ‖𝐙‖F2=tr⁡(𝐙𝐙⊤)\|\mathbf{Z}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}) and 𝚺𝐱1/2​𝚺𝐱1/2=𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}},

‖𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=tr⁡((𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2)​(𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2)⊤)=tr⁡(𝐌​𝚺𝐱​𝐌⊤).□\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl((\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2})(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2})^{\top}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{M}^{\top}).\quad\square

Distribution-weighted risk equals the Frobenius norm of the right-whitened residual 𝐌​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{M}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}.

Lemma A.2.2 (Nonzero-mean inputs).

In this subsection, we decompose the risk for 𝔼⁡[𝐱]≠𝟎\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}]\neq\mathbf{0} into a covariance term and a deterministic mean term, showing 𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22=tr⁡(𝐌​Cov​(𝐱)​𝐌⊤)+‖𝐌​𝝁‖22\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{M}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{M}^{\top})+\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2} (cf. Anderson (1984); Bishop (2006)).

Let 𝝁:=𝔼⁡[𝐱]\bm{\mu}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] and Cov⁡(𝐱):=𝔼⁡[(𝐱−𝝁)​(𝐱−𝝁)⊤]\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu})(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu})^{\top}]. Then

𝔼​‖𝐌𝐱‖22=tr⁡(𝐌​Cov​(𝐱)​𝐌⊤)+‖𝐌​𝝁‖22.\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\mathbf{M}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{M}^{\top}\bigr)+\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}.
Proof.

Write 𝐱=(𝐱−𝝁)+𝝁\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu})+\bm{\mu} and expand:

‖𝐌𝐱‖22=‖𝐌⁡(𝐱−𝝁)‖22+2​⟨𝐌⁡(𝐱−𝝁),𝐌​𝝁⟩+‖𝐌​𝝁‖22.\|\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu})\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu}),\mathbf{M}\bm{\mu}\rangle+\|\mathbf{M}\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}.

Taking expectations annihilates the cross term since 𝔼⁡[𝐱−𝝁]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu}]=\mathbf{0}, yielding the claim. ∎

Risk decomposes into a covariance term plus a mean-induced term.

Theorem A.2.3 (Variable change and whitening).

In this subsection, we show that right-whitening reduces the covariance-aligned objective to a standard Frobenius low-rank approximation by proving ‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=‖𝐄~−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}=\|\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2} with 𝐄~=𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}, 𝐁^=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} (standard whitening trick; cf. Golub and Van Loan (2013)).

Define

𝐄~:=𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2,𝐀^:=𝐀,𝐁^:=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2.\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}:=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{A}}:=\mathbf{A},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{B}}:=\mathbf{B}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}.

Then

‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=‖𝐄~−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2.\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}=\|\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\,\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

Direct substitution:

𝐄~−𝐀^​𝐁^=𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2−𝐀⁡(𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2)=(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2.\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}-\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2})=(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}.

Taking Frobenius norms yields the identity. ∎

Whitening converts risk minimization into a plain Frobenius factorization.

Lemma A.2.4 (Weighted least squares for 𝑨\bm{A} given 𝑩\bm{B}).

In this subsection, we derive the closed-form weighted least-squares minimizer 𝐀∗=𝐄​𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤​(𝐁​𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤)−1\mathbf{A}^{\ast}=\mathbf{E}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top}(\mathbf{B}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top})^{-1} for fixed 𝐁\mathbf{B}, and interpret the residual as a 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}-weighted right projection ((Golub and Van Loan, 2013, Ch. 5), Björck (1996); matrix derivatives in Petersen and Pedersen (2006)).

Consider

f⁡(𝐀):=‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2.f(\mathbf{A}):=\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}.

Let 𝐄:=𝐄cat\mathbf{E}:=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}, 𝐄∼:=𝐄​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{E}_{\sim}:=\mathbf{E}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}, and 𝐁^:=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widehat{\mathbf{B}}:=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}. Then the unique least-squares minimizer is

𝐀∗=𝐄∼​𝐁^⊤​(𝐁^​𝐁^⊤)−1=𝐄​𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤​(𝐁​𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤)−1.\mathbf{A}^{\ast}=\mathbf{E}_{\sim}\,\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\,\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top})^{-1}=\mathbf{E}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{B}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top})^{-1}.
Proof.

In whitened variables,

f⁡(𝐀)=‖𝐄∼−𝐀​𝐁^‖F2=tr⁡(𝐄∼​𝐄∼⊤)−2​tr⁡(𝐀​𝐁^​𝐄∼⊤)+tr⁡(𝐀⁡(𝐁^​𝐁^⊤)​𝐀⊤).f(\mathbf{A})=\|\mathbf{E}_{\sim}-\mathbf{A}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{E}_{\sim}\mathbf{E}_{\sim}^{\top})-2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\mathbf{E}_{\sim}^{\top})+\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\mathbf{A}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top})\mathbf{A}^{\top}\bigr).

Using ∂∂𝐀​tr⁡(𝐀𝐂𝐀⊤)=2​𝐀​𝐂\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{A}}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}^{\top})=2\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{C} for symmetric 𝐂\mathbf{C} and ∂∂𝐀​tr⁡(𝐀𝐌)=𝐌⊤\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{A}}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{M}^{\top} Petersen and Pedersen (2006),

∇𝐀f​(𝐀)=−2​𝐄∼​𝐁^⊤+2​𝐀​(𝐁^​𝐁^⊤)=0⇒𝐀∗=𝐄∼​𝐁^⊤​(𝐁^​𝐁^⊤)−1.\nabla_{\mathbf{A}}f(\mathbf{A})=-2\mathbf{E}_{\sim}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}+2\mathbf{A}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top})=0\;\Rightarrow\;\mathbf{A}^{\ast}=\mathbf{E}_{\sim}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top})^{-1}.

Substituting 𝐄∼=𝐄​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{E}_{\sim}=\mathbf{E}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} and 𝐁^=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} gives the second form. ∎

In whitened variables, 𝐄∼−𝐀∗​𝐁^=𝐄∼​(𝐈−𝐏𝐒^)\mathbf{E}_{\sim}-\mathbf{A}^{\ast}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{E}_{\sim}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\widehat{\mathbf{S}}}) with 𝐏𝐒^:=𝐁^⊤​(𝐁^​𝐁^⊤)−1​𝐁^\mathbf{P}_{\widehat{\mathbf{S}}}:=\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top})^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}, the orthogonal projector onto row⁡(𝐁^)\mathrm{row}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}) in the Euclidean metric. In original variables, 𝐀∗​𝐁=𝐄​𝐏𝚺\mathbf{A}^{\ast}\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{E}\,\mathbf{P}_{\bm{\Sigma}} with

𝐏𝚺:=𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤​(𝐁​𝚺𝐱​𝐁⊤)−1​𝐁,\mathbf{P}_{\bm{\Sigma}}:=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{B}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{B}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{B},

the right projection under the 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}-weighted inner product (a standard form of weighted/oblique projection;( cf. Golub and Van Loan (2013), Ben-Israel and Greville (2010); Björck (1996)).

For fixed 𝐁\mathbf{B}, the optimal 𝐀\mathbf{A} is a weighted LS solution; the residual is a 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}-weighted right projection.

Theorem A.2.5 (Global minimizer; balanced factors; right subspace).

In this subsection, we obtain the global solution via the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960), choose balanced factors 𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓1/2\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}, 𝐁^⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2​𝐕𝒓⊤\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}, and identify the optimal shared right subspace as row(𝐁⋆)=row(𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})=\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}) (cf. Ky Fan’s principle and the subspace discussion in Fan (1950); Golub and Van Loan (2013)).

Let 𝐄~=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} be an SVD and (𝐔𝒓,𝚺𝒓,𝐕𝒓)(\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}) the top-𝒓\bm{r} blocks. Then

𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓1/2,𝐁^⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2​𝐕𝒓⊤\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}

achieve the global optimum of min𝐀^,𝐁^⁡‖𝐄~−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2\min_{\widehat{\mathbf{A}},\widehat{\mathbf{B}}}\|\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}, with minimum value ∑i>𝒓σi​(𝐄~)2\sum_{i>\bm{r}}\sigma_{i}(\widetilde{\mathbf{E}})^{2} Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960); Golub and Van Loan (2013). In original variables,

𝐀⋆=𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓𝚺𝒓1/2,𝐁⋆=𝐁^⋆𝚺𝐱−1/2=𝚺𝒓1/2𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2,\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2},\qquad\mathbf{B}^{\star}=\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2},

and

row(𝐁⋆)=row(𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2).\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})=\mathrm{row}\bigl(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}\bigr).
Proof.

By Theorem A.2.3,

min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=min𝐀^,𝐁^⁡‖𝐄~−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2.\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}=\min_{\widehat{\mathbf{A}},\widehat{\mathbf{B}}}\|\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}.

Left/right orthogonal invariance of the Frobenius norm reduces the problem to minrank⁡(𝐘)≤𝒓⁡‖𝚺−𝐘‖F2\min_{\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{Y})\leq\bm{r}}\|\bm{\Sigma}-\mathbf{Y}\|_{F}^{2}, solved by the truncated SVD 𝐘⋆=𝚺𝒓⊕𝟎\mathbf{Y}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\oplus\mathbf{0}; hence 𝐗⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤\mathbf{X}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top} Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960). Choosing 𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓1/2\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2} and 𝐁^⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2​𝐕𝒓⊤\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top} produces 𝐗⋆=𝐀^⋆​𝐁^⋆\mathbf{X}^{\star}=\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}. Returning to original variables gives the stated (𝐀⋆,𝐁⋆)(\mathbf{A}^{\star},\mathbf{B}^{\star}) and the row-space identity (cf. Fan (1950); Golub and Van Loan (2013)). ∎

In whitened variables: (𝐀^⋆)⊤​𝐀^⋆=𝚺𝒓(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star})^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}} and 𝐁^⋆​(𝐁^⋆)⊤=𝚺𝒓\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star})^{\top}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}. In original variables: (𝐀⋆)⊤​𝐀⋆=𝚺𝒓(\mathbf{A}^{\star})^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}} and 𝐁⋆​𝚺𝐱​(𝐁⋆)⊤=𝚺𝒓\mathbf{B}^{\star}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}} Golub and Van Loan (2013). For any orthogonal 𝐑∈ℝ𝒓×𝒓\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{r}}, (𝐀𝐑,𝐑⊤​𝐁)(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}^{\top}\mathbf{B}) attains the same objective value Golub and Van Loan (2013).

The truncated SVD is globally optimal; the balanced factorization is well-conditioned, and the optimal shared right subspace is row(𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}).

Lemma A.2.6 (Singular 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} and pseudoinverse whitening).

In this subsection, we extend all results to rank-deficient 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} by showing the objective depends only on Range⁡(𝚺𝐱)\mathrm{Range}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}) and that pseudoinverse whitening preserves the conclusions on that subspace Ben-Israel and Greville (2010); Penrose (1955).

Let 𝚺𝐱=𝐐​𝚲​𝐐⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{Q}\bm{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} with 𝚲=diag⁡(λ1,…,λ𝒓+,0,…,0)\bm{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\bm{r}_{+}},0,\dots,0). Define

𝚺𝐱1/2=𝐐𝚲1/2𝐐⊤,𝚺𝐱−1/2=𝐐𝚲†/2𝐐⊤,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}=\mathbf{Q}\bm{\Lambda}^{1/2}\mathbf{Q}^{\top},\qquad\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}=\mathbf{Q}\bm{\Lambda}^{\dagger/2}\mathbf{Q}^{\top},

where 𝚲†/2\bm{\Lambda}^{\dagger/2} applies λi−1/2\lambda_{i}^{-1/2} to λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 and 00 otherwise. Then the objective ‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2} depends only on Range⁡(𝚺𝐱)\mathrm{Range}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}), and Theorems A.2.1–A.2.5 hold unchanged on that subspace.

Proof.

Let 𝐐=[𝐐r​𝐐0]\mathbf{Q}=[\mathbf{Q}_{r}\ \mathbf{Q}_{0}] with 𝐐r\mathbf{Q}_{r} spanning Range⁡(𝚺𝐱)\mathrm{Range}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}) and 𝚺𝐱1/2=𝐐r​𝚲r1/2​𝐐r⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}=\mathbf{Q}_{r}\bm{\Lambda}_{r}^{1/2}\mathbf{Q}_{r}^{\top}. Then

‖(𝐄−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=‖(𝐄𝐐r−𝐀⁡(𝐁𝐐r))​𝚲r1/2‖F2,\|(\mathbf{E}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\|(\mathbf{E}\mathbf{Q}_{r}-\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{Q}_{r}))\bm{\Lambda}_{r}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2},

which is the same Frobenius objective restricted to Range⁡(𝚺𝐱)\mathrm{Range}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}). Components along 𝐐0\mathbf{Q}_{0} vanish under 𝚺𝐱1/2\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} and contribute nothing. ∎

Pseudoinverse whitening discards the nullspace; all conclusions hold on Range⁡(𝚺𝐱)\mathrm{Range}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}).

In our implementation, to estimate and stabilize 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}, we perform ridge/shrinkage regularization (𝚺^𝐱←𝚺^𝐱+ε​𝐈)(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}\leftarrow\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}+\varepsilon\mathbf{I}) while using diagonal approximations (cf. Bishop (2006); Anderson (1984); Ledoit and Wolf (2004); Hoerl and Kennard (2000)) with mini-batch and sliding-window since computing full covariances are costly.

A.3 QR Reduction: Small-Core Equivalence and Global Solution (Proof)

The covariance-aligned objective

min𝐀∈ℝ𝒎×𝒓,𝐁∈ℝ𝒓×𝒅⁡‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2\min_{\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{m}\times\bm{r}},\;\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{d}}}\bigl\|\bigl(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\bigr)\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2} (A.3.1)

can be solved without ever forming the tall whitened matrix 𝐄~:=𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2∈ℝ𝒎×𝒅\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}:=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{m}\times\bm{d}}. A thin QR 𝐄cat=𝐐e​𝐑e\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{R}_{e} (with 𝐐e⊤​𝐐e=𝐈𝒅\mathbf{Q}_{e}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{e}=\mathbf{I}_{\bm{d}}) collects all the information relevant to Eq. A.3.1 into the 𝒅×𝒅\bm{d}\times\bm{d} core 𝐌:=𝐑e​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{M}:=\mathbf{R}_{e}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} because 𝐄~=𝐐e​𝐌\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M} and the Frobenius norm is left-orthogonally invariant (‖𝐐𝐙‖F=‖𝐙‖F\|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Z}\|_{F}=\|\mathbf{Z}\|_{F} when 𝐐⊤​𝐐=𝐈\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{I}) Golub and Van Loan (2013); Trefethen and Bau (1997). Thus we can reduce the large problem to an equivalent 𝒅×𝒅\bm{d}\times\bm{d} problem, apply standard SVD/EYM analysis on the core, and lift the solution back (QR reduction to a core matrix; see also Halko et al. (2011); Martinsson and Tropp (2020) for randomized variants).

Lemma A.3.1 (Optimal 𝑨\bm{A} lies in col⁡(𝐐e)\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{Q}_{e})).

For any 𝐀\mathbf{A}, decompose 𝐀=𝐐e​𝐀^+𝐀⟂\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}+\mathbf{A}_{\perp} with 𝐐e⊤​𝐀⟂=𝟎\mathbf{Q}_{e}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{\perp}=\mathbf{0} and set 𝐁^:=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widehat{\mathbf{B}}:=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}. Then

‖𝐄~−𝐀​𝐁^‖F2=‖𝐐e​(𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^)‖F2+‖𝐀⟂​𝐁^‖F2≥‖𝐐e​(𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^)‖F2,\|\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}-\mathbf{A}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}=\|\mathbf{Q}_{e}(\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}})\|_{F}^{2}+\|\mathbf{A}_{\perp}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2}\;\geq\;\|\mathbf{Q}_{e}(\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}})\|_{F}^{2},

where 𝐄~=𝐐e​𝐌\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M} and 𝐌:=𝐑e​𝚺𝐱1/2\mathbf{M}:=\mathbf{R}_{e}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}. Hence any global minimizer satisfies 𝐀⟂=𝟎\mathbf{A}_{\perp}=\mathbf{0}, i.e., 𝐀⋆=𝐐e​𝐀^⋆\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}. It shrinks the search space for 𝐀\mathbf{A} to the 𝒅\bm{d}-dimensional column space of 𝐐e\mathbf{Q}_{e}; any component orthogonal to col⁡(𝐐e)\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{Q}_{e}) only increases the loss. (Orthogonal decomposition/Pythagorean property of the Frobenius inner product; cf. Golub and Van Loan (2013); Trefethen and Bau (1997).)

Proof.

Use 𝐄~=𝐐e​𝐌\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M} and orthogonality: 𝐐e⊤​(𝐐e​(⋅))=(⋅)\mathbf{Q}_{e}^{\top}(\mathbf{Q}_{e}(\cdot))=(\cdot) and 𝐐e⊤​(𝐀⟂​𝐁^)=𝟎\mathbf{Q}_{e}^{\top}(\mathbf{A}_{\perp}\widehat{\mathbf{B}})=\mathbf{0}, so the two terms are orthogonal in the Frobenius inner product and the squared norm splits. The minimum occurs at 𝐀⟂=𝟎\mathbf{A}_{\perp}=\mathbf{0}. □\square

Theorem A.3.2 (Core equivalence).

By Lemma A.3.1 and left-orthogonal invariance of ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} (i.e., ‖𝐐𝐙‖F=‖𝐙‖F\|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Z}\|_{F}=\|\mathbf{Z}\|_{F} for orthogonal 𝐐\mathbf{Q};  Golub and Van Loan (2013)),

min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2=min𝐀^,𝐁^⁡‖𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2,𝐌=𝐑e​𝚺𝐱1/2.\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\bigl\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}\;=\;\min_{\widehat{\mathbf{A}},\widehat{\mathbf{B}}}\,\|\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{R}_{e}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}. (A.3.2)

Any minimizer (𝐀^⋆,𝐁^⋆)(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star},\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}) lifts to a minimizer of the original problem via

𝐀⋆=𝐐e𝐀^⋆,𝐁⋆=𝐁^⋆𝚺𝐱−1/2,\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star},\qquad\mathbf{B}^{\star}=\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}, (A.3.3)

where 𝚺𝐱−1/2\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2} denotes a (pseudo-)inverse square root when 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} is singular Ben-Israel and Greville (2010).

Proof.

Restrict to 𝐀=𝐐e​𝐀^\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\widehat{\mathbf{A}} (Eq. A.3.3). Then ‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F=‖𝐐e​(𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^)‖F=‖𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F\|(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\|_{F}=\|\mathbf{Q}_{e}(\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}})\|_{F}=\|\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}. The lifting follows by inverting the change 𝐁^=𝐁​𝚺𝐱1/2\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}. □\square

Corollary A.3.3 (Preservation of nonzero singular values and right singular vectors).

Since (𝐐e​𝐌)⊤​(𝐐e​𝐌)=𝐌⊤​𝐌(\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M})^{\top}(\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{M}, 𝐄~=𝐐e​𝐌\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M} and 𝐌\mathbf{M} share the same nonzero singular values and the same right singular vectors. Hence the SVD of 𝐌\mathbf{M} directly yields the optimal shared right subspace for the covariance-aligned objective (orthogonal invariance of SVD; e.g., Golub and Van Loan (2013); Trefethen and Bau (1997)).

Proof.

Immediate from 𝐐e⊤​𝐐e=𝐈𝒅\mathbf{Q}_{e}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{e}=\mathbf{I}_{\bm{d}}. □\square

Theorem A.3.4 (Balanced factors, global minimizer, and lifting).

Let 𝐌=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} be an SVD and (𝐔𝒓,𝚺𝒓,𝐕𝒓)(\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}) the top-𝒓\bm{r} blocks. Then

𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓1/2,𝐁^⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2​𝐕𝒓⊤\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top} (A.3.4)

achieve the global minimum of ‖𝐌−𝐀^​𝐁^‖F2\|\mathbf{M}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\|_{F}^{2} by the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem Eckart and Young (1936); MIRSKY (1960); Golub and Van Loan (2013). Lifting to the original variables gives

𝐀⋆=𝐐e𝐔𝒓𝚺𝒓1/2,𝐁⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2.\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2},\qquad\mathbf{B}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}. (A.3.5)

The minimum value is ‖𝐌−𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤‖F2\|\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}, and the shared right subspace is row(𝐁⋆)=span(𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}) (cf. Ky Fan Fan (1950)).

It provides a closed-form global minimizer and a numerically well-conditioned (balanced) factorization.

Truncated SVD is optimal; balancing (𝚺𝒓1/2)(\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}) improves conditioning and scale regularity Golub and Van Loan (2013).

Proof.

Apply EYM to the core problem from Eq. A.3.2; choose balanced factors so that 𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤=𝐀^⋆​𝐁^⋆\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}=\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}. Use Eq. A.3.3 to obtain (𝐀⋆,𝐁⋆)(\mathbf{A}^{\star},\mathbf{B}^{\star}). □\square

This process makes the thin QR cost 𝒪⁡(𝒎​𝒅 2)\mathcal{O}(\bm{m}\bm{d}^{\,2}), while forming/using the core costs 𝒪⁡(𝒅 3)\mathcal{O}(\bm{d}^{\,3}) (or 𝒪⁡(𝒅 2)\mathcal{O}(\bm{d}^{\,2}) if 𝚺𝐱1/2\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} is precomputed/structured). All subsequent optimization is on the 𝒅×𝒅\bm{d}\times\bm{d} core Golub and Van Loan (2013); Trefethen and Bau (1997). After computing 𝐌\mathbf{M}, we do not materialize 𝐌\mathbf{M}; instead we keep 𝐳↦𝐌𝐳=𝐑e​(𝚺𝐱1/2​𝐳)\mathbf{z}\mapsto\mathbf{M}\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{R}_{e}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\mathbf{z}) and 𝐲↦𝐌⊤​𝐲=𝚺𝐱1/2​(𝐑e⊤​𝐲)\mathbf{y}\mapsto\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{y}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}(\mathbf{R}_{e}^{\top}\mathbf{y}), and pass these to RSVD Halko et al. (2011); Martinsson and Tropp (2020).

From Eq. A.3.5, row(𝐁⋆)=span(𝐕𝒓⊤𝚺𝐱−1/2)\mathrm{row}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})=\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1/2}) defines the shared right subspace. In GlowQ, this subspace is exactly the group-shared projection used to compute and cache 𝐑=𝐁shared​𝐗\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{shared}}\mathbf{X} once per input-sharing group, thereby enabling efficient 𝐀𝒊​𝐑\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}\mathbf{R} reuse during inference while preserving expressivity via module-specific 𝐀𝒊\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}} (cf. Sec. 3.3 and the Ky Fan view in Theorem A.1.3).

A.4 RSVD Accuracy Guarantees

Let the core matrix be 𝐌:=𝐑e​𝚺𝐱1/2∈ℝ𝒅×𝒅\mathbf{M}:=\mathbf{R}_{e}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{d}\times\bm{d}} as defined by the QR reduction in Appendix A.3. We target rank 𝒓≤𝒅\bm{r}\leq\bm{d} with oversampling 𝒑≥2\bm{p}\geq 2 and power iterations 𝒒≥0\bm{q}\geq 0. By the core equivalence and preservation results, accuracy on 𝐌\mathbf{M} transfers verbatim to the covariance-aligned objective.

Algorithm A.4.1 - RSVD on the core 𝐌\mathbf{M}.

It computes the dominant right subspace (which defines the shared right factor) on the small 𝒅×𝒅\bm{d}\times\bm{d} core without ever materializing the tall whitened matrix (standard RSVD; (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020)).

Procedure.
(i) ​𝛀∼𝒩​(0,1)𝒅×(𝒓+𝒑),𝐘←𝐌​𝛀;\displaystyle\text{(i) }\bm{\Omega}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{\bm{d}\times(\bm{r}+\bm{p})},\quad\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow\mathbf{M}\bm{\Omega};
(ii) Power iterations: repeat 𝒒 times {𝐘←𝐌(𝐌⊤𝐘)}with re-orthonormalization;\displaystyle\text{(ii) }\text{Power iterations: repeat }\bm{q}\text{ times }\{\,\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{Y})\,\}\ \text{with re-orthonormalization};
(iii) ​𝐐←orth⁡(𝐘),𝐁←𝐐⊤​𝐌;\displaystyle\text{(iii) }\mathbf{Q}\leftarrow\mathrm{orth}(\mathbf{Y}),\quad\mathbf{B}\leftarrow\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{M};
(iv) 𝐁=𝐔~𝚺𝐕⊤,𝐔←𝐐𝐔~;truncate to (𝐔𝒓,𝚺𝒓,𝐕𝒓);\displaystyle\text{(iv) }\mathbf{B}=\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}\,\bm{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{V}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{U}\leftarrow\mathbf{Q}\widetilde{\mathbf{U}};\ \text{truncate to }(\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}},\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}});
(v) Balanced core factors: 𝐀^⋆=𝐔𝒓𝚺𝒓1/2,𝐁^⋆=𝚺𝒓1/2𝐕𝒓⊤.\displaystyle\text{(v) }\text{Balanced core factors: }\ \widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\star}=\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2},\ \widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\star}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}.

Find a good range 𝐐\mathbf{Q} via randomized sketching (with optional power iterations), then refine by a small SVD on 𝐐⊤​𝐌\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{M}. Justification. Within the subspace ℛ⁡(𝐐)\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Q}), the best rank-𝒓\bm{r} approximation is the truncated SVD of 𝐐⊤​𝐌\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{M}; lifting by 𝐐\mathbf{Q} yields 𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top} as the optimal restricted approximation (Golub and Van Loan, 2013, Ch. 2). The randomized sketch ensures (in expectation or with high probability) that ℛ⁡(𝐐)\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Q}) captures the dominant right subspace of 𝐌\mathbf{M} (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020). □\square

Theorem A.4.2 (Frobenius error, expectation).

Let 𝐌=𝐔​𝚺​𝐕⊤\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σ𝒅\sigma_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{\bm{d}}. For 𝒑≥2\bm{p}\geq 2 and 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0,

𝔼​‖𝐌−𝐐𝐐⊤​𝐌‖F≤(1+𝒓𝒑−1)1/2​(∑j>𝒓σj2)1/2.\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\Bigl(1+\frac{\bm{r}}{\bm{p}-1}\Bigr)^{\!1/2}\,\Bigl(\sum_{j>\bm{r}}\sigma_{j}^{2}\Bigr)^{\!1/2}. (A.4.1)

(Halko–Martinsson–Tropp; e.g., (Halko et al., 2011, Thm. 10.5))

It quantifies that RSVD matches the optimal tail energy up to a mild factor depending only on (𝒓,𝒑)(\bm{r},\bm{p}).

Proof.

Write 𝐌=𝐔​[𝚺1𝟎𝟎𝚺2]​𝐕⊤\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{U}\!\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&\mathbf{0}\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{0}&\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\!\mathbf{V}^{\top} with 𝚺1∈ℝ𝒓×𝒓\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{r}} and 𝚺2\bm{\Sigma}_{2} the tail. Let 𝐕⊤​𝛀=[𝛀1𝛀2]\mathbf{V}^{\top}\bm{\Omega}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Omega}_{1}\\ \bm{\Omega}_{2}\end{bmatrix} and 𝐘=𝐌​𝛀\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{M}\bm{\Omega}. Standard analysis of Gaussian sketches gives ‖(𝐈−𝐏𝐐)​𝐌‖F≤‖𝚺2‖F​‖𝛀2​𝛀1†‖F\|(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Q}})\mathbf{M}\|_{F}\leq\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\|_{F}\,\|\bm{\Omega}_{2}\bm{\Omega}_{1}^{\dagger}\|_{F}, and 𝔼​‖𝛀2​𝛀1†‖F2≤𝒓/(𝒑−1)\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\Omega}_{2}\bm{\Omega}_{1}^{\dagger}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\bm{r}/(\bm{p}-1) for 𝒑≥2\bm{p}\geq 2 (Halko et al., 2011). Taking square roots and expectations yields Eq. A.4.1. □\square

Theorem A.4.3 (Spectral error with 𝒒\bm{q} power iterations).

For 𝒒≥0\bm{q}\geq 0 and a modest constant 𝐂𝒓,𝒑\mathbf{C}_{\bm{r},\bm{p}} (depending gently on 𝒓,𝒑\bm{r},\bm{p}),

‖𝐌−𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤‖2≲𝐂𝒓,𝒑 1/(2​𝒒+1)​σ𝒓+1.\|\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\|_{2}\;\lesssim\;\mathbf{C}_{\bm{r},\bm{p}}^{\,1/(2\bm{q}+1)}\ \sigma_{\bm{r}+1}. (A.4.2)

(Cf. (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020; Musco and Musco, 2015).)

Power iterations shrink the subspace-angle gap geometrically toward the optimal σ𝒓+1\sigma_{\bm{r}+1} bound.

Each power iteration reduces the gap factor roughly by a (⋅)1/(2​𝒒+1)(\cdot)^{1/(2\bm{q}+1)} exponent toward σ𝒓+1\sigma_{\bm{r}+1}.

Proof.

After 𝒒\bm{q} power steps, 𝐘=(𝐌𝐌⊤)𝒒​𝐌​𝛀=𝐔​𝚺 2​𝒒+1​(𝐕⊤​𝛀)\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}^{\top})^{\bm{q}}\mathbf{M}\bm{\Omega}=\mathbf{U}\,\bm{\Sigma}^{\,2\bm{q}+1}(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\bm{\Omega}). Block-partitioning 𝐕⊤​𝛀=[𝛀1𝛀2]\mathbf{V}^{\top}\bm{\Omega}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Omega}_{1}\\ \bm{\Omega}_{2}\end{bmatrix} and analyzing principal angles between the exact and sketched right subspaces gives

‖(𝐈−𝐏𝐐)​𝐌‖2≤‖𝚺2‖2​‖𝚺2 2​𝒒​𝛀2​(𝛀1)†​𝚺1−2​𝒒‖21/(2​𝒒+1).\|(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Q}})\mathbf{M}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\|_{2}\,\Big\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}^{\,2\bm{q}}\bm{\Omega}_{2}(\bm{\Omega}_{1})^{\dagger}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{-2\bm{q}}\Big\|_{2}^{\!1/(2\bm{q}+1)}.

Bounding the Gaussian pseudo-inverse term by 𝐂𝒓,𝒑\mathbf{C}_{\bm{r},\bm{p}} and using ‖𝚺2 2​𝒒​𝚺1−2​𝒒‖2=(σ𝒓+1/σ𝒓)2​𝒒\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}^{\,2\bm{q}}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{-2\bm{q}}\|_{2}=(\sigma_{\bm{r}+1}/\sigma_{\bm{r}})^{2\bm{q}} yields Eq. A.4.2. □\square

Corollary A.4.4 (Transfer to the covariance-aligned objective).

By Theorem A.3.2 and Corollary A.3.3.

‖(𝐄cat−𝐀⋆​𝐁⋆)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F=‖𝐌−𝐔𝒓​𝚺𝒓​𝐕𝒓⊤‖F.\big\|\,(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}^{\star}\mathbf{B}^{\star})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\big\|_{F}\;=\;\|\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{U}_{\bm{r}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{r}}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\|_{F}. (A.4.3)

It links RSVD accuracy on the core directly to the original covariance-aligned objective.

Core RSVD error bounds become the error bounds for the original problem, verbatim.

Proof. We have 𝐄~=𝐄cat​𝚺𝐱1/2=𝐐e​𝐌\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}=\mathbf{Q}_{e}\mathbf{M} and Frobenius norms are left-orthogonally invariant; the optimal truncated approximation on 𝐌\mathbf{M} corresponds under lifting to the optimal approximation of (𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}, yielding Eq. A.4.3. □\square

Proposition (Q-less lifting: blockwise recovery of 𝐀𝒊⋆\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\star}).

Write 𝐄cat=[𝐄1;…;𝐄𝒎]\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=[\mathbf{E}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{E}_{\bm{m}}] and 𝐀⋆=[𝐀1⋆;…;𝐀𝒎⋆]\mathbf{A}^{\star}=[\mathbf{A}_{1}^{\star};\dots;\mathbf{A}_{\bm{m}}^{\star}] conformably. At fixed 𝐁⋆\mathbf{B}^{\star}, each block admits the closed form

𝐀𝒊⋆=𝐄𝒊(𝐁⋆)⊤(𝐁⋆(𝐁⋆)⊤)†,𝒊=1,…,𝒎,\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\star}\;=\;\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{B}^{\star}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}\bigr)^{\bm{\dagger}},\qquad\bm{i}=1,\dots,\bm{m}, (A.4.4)

so the tall orthonormal factor 𝐐e\mathbf{Q}_{e} need not be stored (least-squares with pseudoinverse; cf. (Björck, 1996; Ben-Israel and Greville, 2010; Golub and Van Loan, 2013)).

It economizes memory: per-block factors are recovered directly from (𝐄𝒊,𝐁⋆)(\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}},\mathbf{B}^{\star}) without retaining 𝐐e\mathbf{Q}_{e}.

Per-block least-squares with a pseudoinverse yields 𝐀𝒊⋆\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\star} using only (𝐄𝒊,𝐁⋆)(\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}},\mathbf{B}^{\star}).

Proof. For each block, minimize ‖𝐄𝒊−𝐀𝒊​𝐁⋆‖F2\|\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}-\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}\mathbf{B}^{\star}\|_{F}^{2}. The first-order optimality condition is 𝐀𝒊⋆​𝐁⋆​(𝐁⋆)⊤=𝐄𝒊​(𝐁⋆)⊤\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\star}\mathbf{B}^{\star}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}=\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}. Multiplying on the right by the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse gives the minimal-norm solution 𝐀𝒊⋆=𝐄𝒊​(𝐁⋆)⊤​(𝐁⋆​(𝐁⋆)⊤)†\mathbf{A}_{\bm{i}}^{\star}=\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{B}^{\star}(\mathbf{B}^{\star})^{\top}\bigr)^{\bm{\dagger}}, which is precisely Eq. A.4.4. □\square

Appendix B Effect of right-weighted shared B

In this section, we analyze the effect of the right-weighted shared-B on the GlowQ’s error correction with the following procedure.

Procedure.

(1) Using calibration inputs {𝐱𝒏}𝒏=1𝑵⊂ℝ𝒅\{\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}\}_{\bm{n}=1}^{\bm{N}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{\bm{d}}, estimate the layer input covariance

𝚺^𝐱=1𝑵∑𝒏𝐱𝒏𝐱𝒏⊤(optionally: 𝚺^𝐱←𝚺^𝐱+𝜺𝐈).\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}=\tfrac{1}{\bm{N}}\sum_{\bm{n}}\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}\mathbf{x}_{\bm{n}}^{\top}\quad\text{(optionally: }\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}\!\leftarrow\!\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}+\bm{\varepsilon}\,\mathbf{I}\text{)}.

(2) For each module 𝒊∈{q,k,v,gate,up}\bm{i}\in\{\mathrm{q,k,v,gate,up}\}, form the quantization-error matrix 𝐄𝒊∈ℝ𝑶𝒊×𝒅\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{O}_{\bm{i}}\times\bm{d}} and the row-stack 𝐄cat=[𝐄1;…;𝐄𝒎]∈ℝ𝒎×𝒅\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}=[\mathbf{E}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{E}_{\bm{m}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{m}\times\bm{d}}.

(3) Cov-aligned (whitened): compute SVDs of 𝐄~𝒊:=𝐄𝒊​𝚺^𝐱1/2\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\bm{i}}:=\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2} and 𝐄~cat:=𝐄cat​𝚺^𝐱1/2\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{cat}}:=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}, and take the top-𝒓\bm{r} right bases 𝐕𝒊,𝒓\mathbf{V}_{\bm{i},\bm{r}} and 𝐕𝒓\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}.

(4) Unweighted (no-cov): repeat the same without whitening to obtain 𝐕𝒊,𝒓(no-cov)\mathbf{V}_{\bm{i},\bm{r}}^{\text{(no-cov)}} and 𝐕𝒓(no-cov)\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\text{(no-cov)}}.

(5) For each module, form the absolute cross-basis cosine matrix

𝐂𝒊=|𝐕𝒓⊤​𝐕𝒊,𝒓|∈ℝ𝒓×𝒓,\mathbf{C}_{\bm{i}}\;=\;\bigl|\mathbf{V}_{\bm{r}}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{\bm{i},\bm{r}}\bigr|\in\mathbb{R}^{\bm{r}\times\bm{r}},

Hungarian-reorder it to maximize the diagonal sum, and visualize as heatmaps.

Impact of optimization with the right weighted objective.

As illustrated in Fig. 5 and 6, the whitened condition produces a bright near-diagonal across all groups (Q/K/V and MLP gate/up), indicating a one-to-one alignment between the shared right subspace row⁡(Bshared)\mathrm{row}(B_{\text{shared}}) and each module’s right subspace (up to sign/permutation). The effect is strongest for Q/K, and slightly more diffuse for V and for MLP (gate/up), but remains concentrated on the leading axes. In contrast, the unweighted condition yields noise-like patterns with no diagonal structure.

Right-side covariance weighting is crucial for estimating a shared BB under anisotropic inputs: it exposes a common right subspace across modules that ingest the same input tensor. This validates the shared-BB assumption and directly motivates our ABx caching strategy, i.e., computing R=Bshared​XR=B_{\text{shared}}X once per group and reusing Ai​RA_{i}R across modules. Unweighted stacked SVD fails to reveal this alignment, weakening both the shared-BB premise and the practical caching benefit.

B.1 Group-cached (weighted stacked RSVD) vs. Layer-wise (weighted RSVD)

Results on Table 7.

Across 13 model-size combinations, GlowQ and Layer-wise yield essentially identical perplexity: the mean gap is +0.001 ppl on average, with per-family fluctuations confined to ±0.02\pm 0.02 ppl. By design, GlowQ-S (Selective restore) trades a bit of accuracy for efficiency, trailing Layer-wise by +0.04 ppl on average. In short, the full shared-𝐁\mathbf{B} configuration matches layer-wise (𝐀i,𝐁i)(\mathbf{A}_{i},\mathbf{B}_{i}) on WikiText-2 without systematic degradation, while the selective variant incurs a small, consistent increase in ppl.

Observation on Fig. 5,  6.

The covariance-aligned cross-basis heatmaps exhibit an almost perfectly diagonal structure after Hungarian matching, indicating a near one-to-one correspondence between the shared right subspace and each module’s top-rr directions. Whitening aligns input usage so that the shared 𝐁\mathbf{B} spans (practically) the same right-singular space that the individual 𝐁i\mathbf{B}_{i} would select, explaining why GlowQ’s perplexity tracks layerwise so closely, and why GlowQ-S, restoring only a subset, shows the small upward shift in ppl.

Observation on Fig. 7, 8, 9.

For the MoE FFN of Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the covariance-aligned cross-basis heatmaps show the same qualitative behavior as in the dense models once whitening is enabled. Without whitening, all panels (expert gate/up, shared gate/up, and MoE attention) look almost uniformly dark, indicating that the shared right subspace and each expert’s local top-rr directions are essentially uncorrelated. After whitening and Hungarian matching, the heatmaps become sharply diagonal for both the representative expert (e.g., expert59_gate_proj / expert59_up_proj) and the shared-BB MLP/attention blocks, revealing a near one-to-one alignment between the shared basis and each expert’s own error subspace. This confirms that, once inputs are whitened, the grouped MoE FFNs and the shared MLP effectively live in the same right-singular space, so a single shared 𝐁shared\mathbf{B}_{\text{shared}} can serve all experts with only small residual mismatch. Consequently, GlowQ can compress all experts and the shared MLP with one shared right-hand matrix while closely tracking the layerwise baseline in perplexity, explaining the tiny +0.02 PPL gap we observe on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B.

Appendix C TTFB & Throughput around other models

Results on Table 8.

Table 8 mirrors the LLaMA 2 evaluation under an identical runtime and measurement protocol. Two consistent trends emerge: (i) GlowQ reduces all latency components, with the largest relative gains on per-token decode; and (ii) GlowQ-S further amplifies these benefits. On LLaMA 3 (3.2-3B, 3.1-8B), GlowQ with BX caching improves serving latency over Layerwise: TTFB −9.38%-9.38\%, tok/s +8.00%+8.00\%, Prefill −6.41%-6.41\%, and Dec −8.77%-8.77\% on average. GlowQ-S (selective restore) amplifies these gains: TTFB −25.32%-25.32\%, tok/s +27.52%+27.52\%, Prefill −18.91%-18.91\%, and Dec −24.13%-24.13\% on average. Improvements are consistent across both model sizes, with the largest reductions appearing in the per-token Dec phase and end-to-end TTFB, reflecting reduced compute on the critical path. In practice, BX caching provides drop-in speedups without modifying weights, while the selective policy (GlowQ-S) offers a simple accuracy-latency knob by reducing the number of 𝐀i​𝐑\mathbf{A}_{i}\mathbf{R} applications (Sec. 3.3).

Observation on Table 8.

BX caching removes redundant right-projection work by reusing the shared subspace, so each decode step primarily executes lightweight 𝐀i​𝐑\mathbf{A}_{i}\mathbf{R} updates; this directly lowers Dec and TTFB. The selective-restore strategy further trims the executed paths across decoder blocks, yielding additional latency drops with a commensurate increase in throughput (tok/s). These mechanisms explain the near-linear percentage gains in the RSVD-driven core cost: caching reduces repeated right-side multiplies, while selective restoration shortens the active compute graph along the decoding trajectory.

Appendix D Hyperparameter Change

D.1 Calibration difference

Fig. 10(a),  10(b) plot energy-capture curves versus rank for different numbers of calibration samples, while Fig. 10(c) reports the mean pairwise cosine similarity (weighted) between the shared right subspace and the per-layer right subspaces as the calibration size varies.

Varying the number of calibration samples 𝑵∈{32,64,128,256}\bm{N}\in\{32,64,128,256\} leaves the energy-capture curves in Fig. 10(a),  10(b) nearly indistinguishable, especially for practical ranks 𝒓≤128\bm{r}\!\leq\!128. In Fig. 10(c), the weighted cosine similarity between the shared right subspace and layer-wise right subspaces is already high at 𝑵=32\bm{N}=32 and saturates for 𝑵≥64\bm{N}\geq 64. These results indicate that a small calibration set suffices to recover a stable, data-aligned right subspace, consistent with PCA stability under a clear spectral gap (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016; Horn and Johnson, 1985).

We attribute the observed stability under a relatively small calibration set, e.g., N=32N=32 to the following four reasons: (i) Spectral-gap effect: The input covariance 𝚺𝐱\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}} is heavy-tailed, so the top directions are separated by a clear eigenvalue gap; the dominant 𝒓\bm{r}-dimensional right subspace stabilizes quickly with modest 𝑵\bm{N} (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016; Horn and Johnson, 1985). (ii) Robust weighted objective. We optimize a right-weighted criterion,

min𝐀,𝐁⁡‖(𝐄cat−𝐀𝐁)​𝚺𝐱1/2‖F2,\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\ \bigl\|\bigl(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cat}}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\bigr)\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{F}^{2},

so small perturbations in the estimate 𝚺^𝐱\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}} have limited effect: large-eigenvalue axes dominate and lead to the same top 𝒓\bm{r}-subspace (see also weighted low-rank formulations (Srebro and Jaakkola, 2003)). Numerical regularization. Shrinkage/normalization of 𝚺^𝐱\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}} reduces small-sample noise and improves conditioning (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004; Hoerl and Kennard, 2000; Bishop, 2006). Benefit of group stacking. Building the SVD core from vertically stacked errors increases the effective sample support along rows, which smooths estimation of the shared right subspace (Paige and Saunders, 1981; Golub and Van Loan, 2013).

To conclude, calibration sizes as small as 𝑵≈32​–​64\bm{N}\approx 32\text{--}64 already place the system in a saturated mode since energy capture at a fixed 𝒓\bm{r} and the similarity between the shared and layer-wise right subspaces change only marginally beyond this point. Thus, our covariance-aligned, group-shared 𝐁\mathbf{B} achieves stable performance with low calibration cost.

D.1.1 Shrink Alpha Difference

We apply a standard covariance shrinkage when forming the input statistic used for covariance-aligned subspace estimation. Let 𝚺^𝐱\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}} be the sample covariance from 𝑵\bm{N} calibration sequences and 𝒅\bm{d} the input dimension. We construct

𝚺^𝐱(𝜶)=(1−𝜶)​𝚺^𝐱+𝜶​tr⁡(𝚺^𝐱)𝒅​𝐈,𝜶∈[0,1],\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}\;=\;(1-\bm{\alpha})\,\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}\;+\;\bm{\alpha}\,\frac{\mathrm{tr}\!\big(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}\big)}{\bm{d}}\,\mathbf{I},\qquad\bm{\alpha}\in[0,1],

i.e., a convex combination of the sample covariance and an isotropic target (scaled identity); small 𝜶\bm{\alpha} reduces small-sample noise and improves conditioning without altering the dominant axes learned from data (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004; Bishop, 2006; Anderson, 1984).

Results on Table 9.

Across calibration sizes 𝑵∈{32,64,128,256}\bm{N}\in\{32,64,128,256\} and shrink 𝜶∈{0,0.02,0.05}\bm{\alpha}\in\{0,0.02,0.05\}, perplexity remains essentially flat for LLaMA 3: for 3.2-3B and 8B, the sweep changes values by +0.01 ppl on average. Qwen 3 shows the same qualitative behavior, with a mild benefit from shrinkage: 𝜶∈[0.02,0.05]\bm{\alpha}\in[0.02,0.05] yields -0.02 ppl on average for 3.1-8B and -0.01 ppl on average for 14B (relative to 𝜶=0\bm{\alpha}{=}0 at the same 𝑵\bm{N}). Aggregating all models, 𝜶=0.02\bm{\alpha}{=}0.02 improves by -0.01 ppl average, and increasing 𝑵\bm{N} beyond 6464 produces only marginal changes (≤+0.01\leq\,+0.01-+0.02+0.02 ppl on average depending on the family). In short, both the calibration size and a small shrink factor have only second-order effect on WikiText-2 perplexity, consistent with the stability suggested by the energy and cosine-similarity panels (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016).

Observation on Table 9.

The right subspace stabilizes quickly because (i) the input covariance exhibits a pronounced spectral gap, so the dominant 𝒓\bm{r}-dimensional space is identified with few samples (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016; Horn and Johnson, 1985); (ii) the right-weighted objective emphasizes large-variance directions, making the solution insensitive to small perturbations in 𝚺^𝐱\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}}; (iii) mild shrinkage damps small-sample noise (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004; Bishop, 2006); and (iv) stacking modules to form the core increases effective sample support along rows (Paige and Saunders, 1981; Golub and Van Loan, 2013). Consequently, small calibration sets (𝑵≈32​–​64\bm{N}\approx 32\text{--}64) already recover a data-aligned shared right subspace, explaining the near-constant perplexity across the sweep and the slight, consistent gains from 𝜶∈[0.02,0.05]\bm{\alpha}\in[0.02,0.05] on Qwen 3.

D.1.2 Memory usage

Results on Fig. 11.

We profile calibration on a single A100 80GB GPU for three OPT models (6.7B, 13B, 30B) and calibration sizes 𝑵∈{32,64,128}\bm{N}\in\{32,64,128\}, using SlimPajama-6B as the calibration corpus. Fig. 11(a) shows that the total wall-clock time is dominated by the calibration pass: for every model, the blue bars (forward passes used to estimate 𝚺^𝐱\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{x}} and collect error tensors) account for most of the runtime and grow almost linearly with 𝑵\bm{N}, whereas the red bars (randomized GSVD / decomposition) contribute a relatively small and nearly constant overhead. Even for OPT-30B, increasing 𝑵\bm{N} from 3232 to 128128 scales the runtime by roughly the same factor, indicating that the cost is predictable and controlled by the choice of calibration size. Fig. 11(b) breaks down the memory footprint. Peak GPU memory (blue) grows moderately with model size and remains well below the CPU footprint, since we keep the model and activations on GPU but store error and covariance tensors on host memory. The green and purple bars show that these two tensors dominate the CPU usage and scale with model size: moving from OPT-6.7B to OPT-30B increases both err_size and cov_size by several times, and the peak CPU RAM closely tracks their sum.

Observation on Fig. 11.

Overall, the results indicate that the main cost of our method comes from a one-time, embarrassingly parallel calibration phase whose runtime scales linearly with 𝑵\bm{N} and roughly with model size, while the decomposition step has almost fixed cost. Memory-wise, the GPU footprint is modest and does not require larger-than-standard accelerators; the heavy objects are the error and covariance tensors on CPU, which can be streamed, sharded, or discarded immediately after decomposition. Since Sections D.1–D.1.1 show that small calibration sets (𝑵≈32​–​64\bm{N}\approx 32\text{--}64) already yield stable energy capture, right-subspace similarity, and perplexity, practitioners can operate in this low-𝑵\bm{N} regime. In practice, this keeps the calibration overhead to a few GPU hours even for 30B models and confines the CPU memory requirement to a one-off offline preprocessing step, directly addressing concerns about prohibitive calibration time and memory pressure for large LLMs.

D.3 Randomized SVD parameters

D.3.1 Proof of QR reduction & Randomized SVD

Discussion.

Table 11 shows that Exact SVD on the 𝒅×𝒅\bm{d}\times\bm{d} core 𝐌\mathbf{M} takes 42.86 s in total (0.76 s per layer on average), whereas Randomized SVD (RSVD) completes in 5.16–5.22 s (0.09 s per layer). This ≈8.2\approx\!8.2–8.3×8.3\times wall-clock speedup is consistent with the complexity gap between 𝒪⁡(𝒅3)\mathcal{O}(\bm{d}^{3}) and 𝒪⁡((𝒒+1)​𝒅2​(𝒓+𝒑)+𝒅​(𝒓+𝒑)2)\mathcal{O}\!\big((\bm{q}{+}1)\,\bm{d}^{2}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})+\bm{d}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})^{2}\big) when 𝒅≫𝒓+𝒑\bm{d}\gg\bm{r}{+}\bm{p} (Golub and Van Loan, 2013; Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020). Concretely, with 𝒅=3072\bm{d}{=}3072, 𝒓=64\bm{r}{=}64, and 𝒑∈{0,…,24}\bm{p}\!\in\!\{0,\dots,24\}, we have (𝒓+𝒑)/𝒅≤88/3072≈2.9%(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})/\bm{d}\leq 88/3072\approx 2.9\%, so the RSVD term (𝒒+1)​𝒅2​(𝒓+𝒑)(\bm{q}{+}1)\,\bm{d}^{2}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p}) scales roughly like a few percent of 𝒅3\bm{d}^{3} up to constant factors, matching the observed order-of-magnitude reduction in runtime.

Effect of q\bm{q} and p\bm{p}. Runtime varies only weakly across 𝒑∈{0,4,8,16,24}\bm{p}\in\{0,4,8,16,24\} and 𝒒∈{0,1,2}\bm{q}\in\{0,1,2\} (5.16 s →\to 5.22 s). This is expected because the dominant RSVD cost is the matrix-block multiplies 𝐌​𝛀,𝐌⊤​(⋅)\mathbf{M}\bm{\Omega},\ \mathbf{M}^{\top}(\cdot); increasing 𝒑\bm{p} from 00 to 2424 changes (𝒓+𝒑)(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p}) from 6464 to 8888 (only ∼38%\sim\!38\%), and the extra 𝒒\bm{q} passes add a small multiple of the same GEMM cost. The lower-order term 𝒅​(𝒓+𝒑)2\bm{d}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})^{2} is negligible at this scale. In short, the linear dependence on (𝒓+𝒑)(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p}) and on (𝒒+1)(\bm{q}{+}1) predicted by

𝒪⁡((𝒒+1)​𝒅2​(𝒓+𝒑)+𝒅​(𝒓+𝒑)2)\mathcal{O}\!\big((\bm{q}{+}1)\,\bm{d}^{2}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})+\bm{d}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})^{2}\big)

manifests as a near-flat runtime curve because 𝒅≫𝒓+𝒑\bm{d}\gg\bm{r}{+}\bm{p} and GEMM kernels saturate the device (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020).

Accuracy. Perplexity stays essentially unchanged: Exact == 8.16; RSVD is 8.228.22 at (𝒒=0,𝒑=0)(\bm{q}{=}0,\bm{p}{=}0) and improves to 8.15​–​8.168.15\text{--}8.16 for 𝒒≥1\bm{q}\!\geq\!1 (with small 𝒑\bm{p} already sufficient). This aligns with randomized SVD theory: even a single power iteration (𝒒=1\bm{q}{=}1) sharpens separation between leading and trailing singular directions and yields a right subspace that is effectively indistinguishable (for a rank-𝒓\bm{r} objective) from Exact SVD in downstream perplexity (Halko et al., 2011; Musco and Musco, 2015; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020).

The empirical results agree with the stated complexity: Exact SVD on 𝐌\mathbf{M} incurs 𝒪⁡(𝒅3)\mathcal{O}(\bm{d}^{3}) time, while RSVD retrieves the leading right subspace in 𝒪⁡((𝒒+1)​𝒅2​(𝒓+𝒑))\mathcal{O}\!\big((\bm{q}{+}1)\,\bm{d}^{2}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})\big) time (plus a minor 𝒅​(𝒓+𝒑)2\bm{d}(\bm{r}{+}\bm{p})^{2} term) (Golub and Van Loan, 2013; Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020). In practice, 𝒒=1\bm{q}{=}1 with a modest 𝒑\bm{p} (e.g., 𝒑∈[4,16]\bm{p}\in[4,16]) delivers near-Exact perplexity at ∼8×\sim\!8\times lower wall time, and increasing 𝒑\bm{p} further yields diminishing returns (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020).

D.3.2 Power iteration & Oversampling difference

Table 12 contrasts oversampling 𝒑\bm{p} (with 𝒒=2\bm{q}{=}2 fixed; subtable 12(a)) and power iterations 𝒒\bm{q} (with 𝒑=16\bm{p}{=}16 fixed; subtable 12(b)). Empirically, increasing 𝒑\bm{p} from 1010 to 2424 leaves PPL essentially unchanged across models (differences of ≤0.01\leq 0.01), whereas raising 𝒒\bm{q} from 00 to 11 yields small but consistent gains (most visibly on Qwen3–8B), after which improvements saturate by 𝒒=2\bm{q}{=}2.

This pattern aligns with the standard analysis of randomized SVD (RSVD). Oversampling enlarges the sketch dimension to ℓ=𝒓+𝒑\bm{\ell}=\bm{r}+\bm{p}, which reduces the probability of missing near-rank-𝒓\bm{r} directions but ultimately does not change the target truncation rank 𝒓\bm{r}. Once 𝒓\bm{r} already captures the dominant subspace and the spectral gap is reasonable, the marginal benefit of additional 𝒑\bm{p} is small; theory predicts only a mild reduction of the residual as 𝒑\bm{p} grows (e.g., with expected error bounds that degrade roughly as 𝒓/(𝒑−1)\sqrt{\bm{r}/(\bm{p}-1)}), so practical guidance typically recommends 𝒑≈5​–​10\bm{p}\approx 5\text{--}10 (Halko et al., 2011; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020).

By contrast, 𝒒\bm{q} directly amplifies spectral separation via the power scheme. Forming 𝐘=(𝐀𝐀⊤)𝒒​𝐀​𝛀\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\top})^{\bm{q}}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega} effectively reweights singular values as σ𝒊 2​𝒒+1\sigma_{\bm{i}}^{\,2\bm{q}+1}, which boosts the ratio between σ𝒓\sigma_{\bm{r}} and the tail {σj>𝒓}\{\sigma_{j>\bm{r}}\} and thereby reduces leakage beyond rank 𝒓\bm{r}. As a result, the sampled subspace aligns better with the true top-𝒓\bm{r} subspace, often yielding noticeable gains from 𝒒=0\bm{q}{=}0 to 𝒒=1\bm{q}{=}1, with diminishing returns thereafter; 𝒒∈{1,2}\bm{q}\in\{1,2\} is commonly recommended in practice (Halko et al., 2011; Ma and Ma, 2024; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020).

When 𝒓\bm{r} already captures the dominant energy, increasing 𝒑\bm{p} beyond a modest buffer offers little accuracy benefit, while a single power iteration (𝒒=1\bm{q}{=}1) can materially improve approximation for matrices with slowly decaying spectra. In our experiments, this theoretical expectation manifests as flat PPL curves across 𝒑\bm{p} and consistent but saturating improvements across 𝒒\bm{q}.

Appendix E Compatibility Across Quantization Datatypes

We apply weight-only quantization to Mistral-7B and evaluate on the WikiText-2 test set across both integer and floating-point-like datatypes (Table 13). For the integer settings (INT2/INT3/INT4), we use uniform weight-only quantization with shared scales within each weight group. For the floating-point-like settings (MXFP4, MXFP6, NVFP4), we adopt microscaling-style formats in which weights are first normalized within a small block and then encoded using low-bit floating-point codes. Concretely, MXFP4 and MXFP6 follow the block-wise microscaling design of MX+ and the OCP MX specification, using a shared scale per block and 4-bit or 6-bit element codes, respectively Lee et al. (2025); Open Compute Project (2023). NVFP4 follows NVIDIA’s reference design with a microscaled FP4 representation for weights, as described in their low-precision inference guidelines Alvarez et al. (2025). These configurations allow us to test GlowQ not only on conventional integer quantization, but also on recent microscaling-based floating-point-like formats.

Layering GlowQ on top of the quant-only baselines reduces perplexity by -991.16 on INT2, -0.32 on INT3, -0.10 on INT4, -1.95 on MXFP4, -0.04 on MXFP6, and -0.46 on NVFP4, relative to the corresponding quant-only settings. Improvements hold across all six evaluated datatypes, indicating that GlowQ behaves as an orthogonal, plug-and-play low-rank correction rather than a mechanism tied to a single integer format or precision; in particular, it remains compatible with recent floating-point-like microscaling formats while providing consistent accuracy gains.

Appendix F LongBench Results

Table 14, 15 shows that across both 4K and 8K context settings on the English LongBench benchmark (Bai et al., 2023b), applying W4 weight quantization with GlowQ (W4A4/8/16+GlowQ) leads to only small differences from the original LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct on the 15 English LongBench tasks. On most tasks, the scores remain within a few points of the baseline, and the relative difficulty and ranking among tasks are largely preserved. This indicates that, even under aggressive quantization of both weights and activations, the low-rank correction in GlowQ keeps the overall performance stable.

When we extend the context length from 4K to 8K, both the baseline and the GlowQ models improve their average scores by a similar margin. In other words, in scenarios that benefit from longer context, the GlowQ models track the same performance trends as the full-precision model, without a collapse in reasoning ability in the long-context regime. Overall, GlowQ enables 4-bit quantization while preserving LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct’s performance not only in standard contexts but also in long-context settings.

Appendix G Selective Restoration across Model Family

Importance metric selection.

The performance of GlowQ-S depends on the policy used to rank groups for restoration. In Fig. 12, we evaluate five saliency metrics from quantization and pruning literature. These include: (1) gsvd singular value sum, our ge​cg_{ec} score (Eq. 9), which measures the captured error “energy” (∥A∥F2\lVert A\rVert_{F}^{2}) in the low-rank factors and follows the standard practice of using singular-value energy to summarize PCA components (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016; Halko et al., 2011); (2) normalized error ratio, our gn​e​rg_{ner} score ( Eq. 10), a widely used PTQ-style proxy based on relative weight error ∥Eg∥F/∥Wg∥F\lVert E_{g}\rVert_{F}/\lVert W_{g}\rVert_{F} (Nagel et al., 2021; Gholami et al., 2021; Krishnamoorthi, 2018); (3) frobenius norm error, the absolute error ∥Eg∥F\lVert E_{g}\rVert_{F} (Nagel et al., 2021; Pouransari et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025); (4) cosine similarity, measuring angular deviation between pre- and post-quantization weights or activations, which has been shown to be a strong pruning/quantization proxy (Mason-Williams and Dahlqvist, 2024; Chang et al., 2023); and (5) layer order as a simple baseline. The results show that gsvd singular value sum and normalized error ratio are consistently the most effective, yielding the steepest perplexity reduction. However, as noted in Sec. 3.3, no single metric is universally optimal. Therefore, our final policy (Sec. 4.6) pragmatically evaluates both ge​cg_{ec} and gn​e​rg_{ner} for a given model and selects the one that performs best, providing a robust, data-driven approach.

Results on Fig. 13.

Across the four panels, LLaMA models exhibit a clear knee: perplexity drops steeply once a relatively small fraction of groups is restored, then plateaus. In contrast, Qwen and OPT show a gradual, near-linear descent as the restored fraction increases. The two evaluation curves in each subplot (ppl_gsvd vs. ppl_NER) track each other closely, differing mainly in the sharpness of the early descent.

These curves suggest selecting the error-recovery metric per model family: outlier/energy ranking with small budgets for knee-shaped profiles, and Hessian-/loss-weighted ranking with broader budgets for diffuse profiles. This family-aware policy aligns with known outlier, anisotropy, and curvature phenomena in modern LLMs.
